title: Bank of California National Ass’n v. Superior Court (1940)
summary: The action could proceed against present estate recipients without necessarily joining every other distributee.
notes:
Read the historical necessary/indispensable language alongside Provident Tradesmens and the modern Rule 19 sequence. An abstract label cannot replace the rule’s practical inquiry.

Sara Boyd died in 1937 leaving an estate of about $225,000; her niece Bertha Smedley sued to enforce Boyd's alleged contract to leave her the entire estate, serving only the Bank of California (executor) and St. Luke's Hospital (the residuary legatee), and the court distinguished 'necessary' parties, who should be joined if possible, from 'indispensable' parties, without whom the action cannot proceed at all.

sections.Parties: The claimant sought to enforce an alleged agreement concerning a decedent’s estate against its executor and recipients of estate property.
sections.Material Facts: The dispute involved an alleged promise to make a testamentary disposition. The plaintiff sought relief against persons who received property instead. A principal residuary recipient received more than seventy-one percent of the estate, while other distributees had separate and sometimes small interests. Some were outside the state or country. The relief against each recipient could operate on that recipient’s property without binding all others.
sections.Procedural History: The California Supreme Court considered a request for a writ of prohibition based on the absence of other distributees. It denied the peremptory writ.
sections.Issue: Did failure to join every distributee make it impossible for the court to proceed?
sections.Holding: No. The absent distributees were not indispensable in the sense necessary to prohibit the action against those present.
sections.Reasoning: The court distinguished the advantage of resolving the entire controversy from the necessity of every interested person’s participation. A decree against a particular recipient could leave others’ rights unadjudicated. Possible delay, the feasibility of obtaining service, and the relative interests could inform a discretionary joinder decision, but did not establish the absolute bar asserted. The court expressly declined to resolve whether the lower court had abused its discretion in refusing broader joinder through the procedural vehicle before it.

learning.why: The action could proceed against present estate recipients without necessarily joining every other distributee.

topics.cp-required-joinder: An interest in the estate did not make every distributee indispensable to relief against the parties already present.
topics.cp-nonparty-protection: The decree could bind the present recipients without adjudicating the rights of absent recipients.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: The Bank of California account distinguishes the power to proceed without particular absent distributees from the discretionary case-management question whether to add available persons.
topics.cp-frcp-19: The necessary-versus-indispensable distinction is the state-law forerunner of the Rule 19(a)/(b) structure.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: The absent distributees could not be joined because many were outside California's reach, which drove the indispensability analysis.

mnemonic.rationale: A promised estate, and who must be joined
